To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the elevated formiminoglutaric acid excretion by tumor-bearing rats could be reversed by the dietary administration of methionine or choline, but not by folate or vitamin B 12.
the folate status of tumor-bearing animals is altered in a way that may be the consequence, in part, of a requirement for methyl groups by the host and/or the tumor.
the folate-deficient state of tumor-bearing animals cannot be reversed by high levels of folate, methionine, or vitamin B 12 in the diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the presence of a tumor on folate metabolism.
the nutritional requirements of the host-tumor systems and the metabolic interrelationships that may exist in these systems.
the effect of the tumor-bearing state on folate and related metabolism in the host.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the folate-deficient state of the tumor-bearing rat is due to an increased requirement for methyl groups by the host-tumor complex.
the folate-deficient tumor-bearing rat is not a useful model for folate-deficient humans.

the elevated urinary formimino glutamic acid excretion of rats bearing the Walker 256 tumor and the Novikof hepatoma is due to a folate deficiency in these animals, which is not due to a dietary deficiency of folate, to altered hepatic folate metabolism, or to a deficiency of vitamin B 1 2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the folate-deficient tumor-bearing animal has a methyl group requirement that is not met by the dietary supply, and that this requirement is not met by any of the known folate cofactors or by the known folate-dependent methyl group donors.
the folate requirement of the host-tumor complex is greater than that of the normal host.
the folate requirement of the host-tumor complex was increased, and this was reflected in the elevated formiminoglutarate excretion of tumor-bearing animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the folate requirement is increased by a factor of 10 or more in the tumor-bearing animal.
the folate status of a host animal can be significantly affected by the presence of a tumor.
the folate status of the host-tumor complex must be considered when evaluating the effects of dietary factors on the tumor-bearing animal.
